The isolated right hemisphere, which is the side of the brain responsible for processing visual information and spatial awareness, may still have some ability to support reading and phonological processing skills after a cerebral hemispherectomy. This surgical procedure involves removing or damaging one or more hemispheres of the brain in an attempt to control seizures associated with very early (in utero) insults.

Research has shown that individuals who undergo cerebral hemispherectomy can still exhibit variability in their cognitive and language abilities, even within groups having similar etiologies and timelines of insult. However, this does not necessarily mean that the isolated right hemisphere will be unable to read or support reading skills.

Studies have found that survivors of lobar intracerebral hemorrhage (ICH) with atrial fibrillation may benefit from long-term anticoagulation therapy, while patients with deep hemispheric ICH at high risk for thromboembolic stroke or low risk of ICH recurrence might also benefit from this treatment.

Regarding the question of whether mental imagery functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) can predict recovery in patients with disorders of consciousness, such as vegetative state (VS), the findings suggest that it may not have a significant prognostic value. However, some patients showed favorable further courses until the end of observation period, and this proposal is made for these patients.

In the case of congenital cardiac surgery, most children can be extubated in the operating room, while many undergoing complex procedures can be extubated within 24 hours after surgery. Early extubation has been associated with low morbidity rates and short lengths of intensive care unit and hospital stays.

Regarding dementia and aphasia in motor neuron disease (MND), there is an underrecognized association between these conditions. Studies have found that the prevalence of cognitive impairment is higher than previously reported, and language deficits, especially anomia, are relatively frequent.

Finally, regarding convulsions and retinal hemorrhage, it may be worth investigating further to rule out other potential causes.

In terms of teaching communication with terminally ill patients, research has shown that courses can lead to relevant changes in communication behavior and self-confidence.
